newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Products Outlook- Gasoline demand keys gains.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Products Outlook- Gasoline demand keys gains.

text.p: Prompt gasoline is likely to see brisk buying, supporting prices through the week, market players forecast Monday.
"They are still tight," said one Gulf player.
"It's been crazy like this since June," seconded another trader, indicating that buyers were still willing to pay high premiums to the NYMEX futures prices to secure barrels.

Gulf conventional gasoline prices remained solidly inside their six-week bullish trend, though prices have dipped modestly from the high of nearly 64.50 cents a gallon seen on July 30. The spot price has rallied about 12.5 cents from the lows seen in June.
Prompt conventional M1 gasoline in the Gulf has held a premium to the NYMEX futures for the past week, a sign of tightness in the spot market, one trader said.
Gulf Coast M1 differentials already jumped about 2.00 cents a gallon by midday Monday, reaching nearly 3.00 cents over the NYMEX September futures after starting the day at a one cent premium.
Analysts have pointed to the strong summer demand, which came late this year, as the main catalyst for the price gains.

The Department of Energy's Energy Information Administration (EIA) put gasoline demand at 8.57 million barrels a day over the past four weeks, an increase of more than 5 percent from the year-ago levels.

News Monday that the United Nations okayed Iraq's aid plan, expected to be followed quickly by a return of Iraqi oil exports after more than two months' absence, should have a very limited effect on the relative strength of U.S. refined products in the near term, analysts said.

The underlying futures prices may rise or fall because of the Iraq news, but market participants said it will have little effect in the near-term on the solid demand that underlies this summer's action in product markets.

New York Harbor traders said they expected gasoline differentials to remain firm this week amid fears of a delay in imports due to production problems. Traders pointed to a possible decline in imports following two refinery outages in Europe and a big fire which is expected to keep PDVSA's 310,000 bpd Curacao plant below capacity for up to two months.
"The key is what happened in Europe. If we lose imports then the strength could be sustained in the next few weeks," said a Harbor broker.

But the broker added it is still not clear whether Harbor players were holding net long or short positions. Valero and Galaxy were heard having commitments to deliver about one million barrels of gasoline against the NYMEX August contract, which reached expiration last week. Speculation that they may have a difficult time coming up with the barrels because of tight supply has helped fuel gains.
"I lot of people are speculating," said a broker, adding the two brokerage houses were seen looking for components to blend their own reformulated gasoline for delivery.
Another broker, however, countered that the two companies have the material, and that the gains were not related to brisk short covering.
